chapter.title: Inspecting the work: the 3 checks before you trust a build

cards.body: The contractor packs up and says "all done." You don't take their word for it. You walk the room, flip the switches, run the taps. You ask what they did today and why. Then you add a line to the house notes on the fridge: "no nails in the north wall, there are pipes behind it." Next week's crew reads the notes before they start.

cards.title: Three checks, every time
cards.body:
Claude saying "done" means it finished typing. It does not mean the app works for a real person. So you close every session with 3 checks.

Check 1: walk it. Open the app in your browser and use it like a user, not like a builder. Do the one job the app is for, start to finish. Then try one thing that worked before today, to make sure it still does.

Check 2: read the change list. Ask Claude: "List every file you changed this session, with one line on why." You are looking for surprises: a file you did not expect, or a change you did not ask for.

Check 3: write the rules. Claude Code reads a file called CLAUDE.md (a plain text notes file) from your project folder at the start of each session. Put 3 to 5 house rules in it. Next session, the builder starts already knowing them.

The order matters a little. Test first, because the test tells you what to ask about. Rules last, because the session tells you which rules were missing.

cards.prompt: Claude says: "Done, the delete button now works." What do you do first?

options.text: Ask Claude to list what it changed.
Open the app and click delete yourself.
Write a rule in CLAUDE.md saying delete must work.

whyNot.a: That's check 2, not check 1: the change list is more useful after you know whether the app actually works.
whyNot.c: That's check 3, not check 1: rules are for next session; right now you need to know if this session's work holds up.

cards.reteach: "Done" is the builder's word, not yours. The first check is always you, in the browser, using the feature like a stranger would. Only after that do you ask what changed and write down lessons.

cards.title: The to-do app and the extra file
cards.body: You asked Claude to add a delete button to your to-do app. It says done. Check 1: you open the app, add "buy milk", click delete, and it disappears. You also tick a task as done, which worked yesterday. Still works. Check 2: you ask for the change list. Claude names 3 files: the page, the logic, and the styling file. You never mentioned styling. Claude explains it changed all the button colors "to match." Check 3: you did not want that, so you add a rule to CLAUDE.md: "Do not change styling unless I ask for it."

cards.title: What goes in the rules file
cards.body:
A rule earns its place when you have said it twice, or when skipping it cost you time. The styling surprise above is a good rule. "Make the app nice" is not a rule, it is a wish.

Good rules are short and checkable. "After every change, tell me how to test it in the browser." "One feature per request; stop and wait after each." "Ask before adding any new tool or service." Each one is a sentence a builder can follow or break, nothing in between.

Keep the file under about 15 lines. A long rules file gets skimmed, by people and by Claude. If you reach 8 rules, cut the ones that have not mattered lately.

The file lives in your project folder, so save it with Git like any other file (chapter 5). Then it travels with the project to GitHub and to any other computer.

cards.prompt: The app works. Claude's change list shows it edited the settings file, which you never mentioned. What is the right move?

options.text: Ignore it. The app works, so the change must be fine.
Ask Claude why it changed that file and whether the change is needed, then decide to keep or undo it.
Delete the settings file so the unasked change is gone.

whyNot.a: That's trusting "done" again, not inspecting: a working app today can hide a settings change that bites you next week.
whyNot.c: That's demolition, not inspection: settings files usually hold things the app needs to start at all. Ask first, then undo only the one change if needed.

cards.reteach: The change list exists so surprises get questioned, not ignored and not panicked over. A surprise file means one question to Claude: "why this, and is it needed?" Then you choose. If the answer is no, Claude can undo just that change, or you restore the last saved version.

cards.body: The mistake is taking "done" as proof. Claude writes "done" when it finishes its own steps, which is not the same as the feature working on your screen. You can spot it in yourself: if you have not opened the app since the last change, you have not checked anything yet. Open it before you reply.

cards.prompt: What are the 3 checks before you trust a build?

options.text: Test it as a user, read Claude's list of changes, write the rules for next time.
Describe the user, the one job, and what done looks like.

whyNot.b: That's the save-point routine from chapter 5, not the inspection: Git keeps versions, it doesn't tell you whether this version works.
whyNot.c: That's the brief from chapter 2, not the inspection: that happens before building, the 3 checks happen after.

cards.reteach: Picture the contractor leaving: you walk the room, you ask what they did, you update the fridge notes. Walk, ask, write. Same three, every session.

cards.body: In your project folder, create a file named CLAUDE.md. Write 3 rules you wish Claude had followed this week. Save it, then start Claude Code and ask: "What rules are you following in this project?"

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now end a session by testing the app yourself, reading what Claude changed, and leaving 3 to 5 rules the builder reads next time.
